title: Chapter 103 – The Gray Peak Road
html:
[Beyond the Northern Gate – Lin Jian]

The back stair of the Sutra Hall smells of nothing at all, and that is the first thing that frightens him.

He goes down it at the third bell of the night, with a shaded lantern in one hand and the brass key in the other, past the lower vault, past the iron door of the Founders' Archive, to a place where the stone wall of the corridor ends in a heap of tumbled rock. Ye did not exaggerate. The slide has been there a hundred years. Moss has grown over the boulders, then died, then grown again. He stands in front of it for a long while with the lantern held low, looking for the seam.

There, says Pebble, from his shoulder. Under. A crack. Small. Door behind.

He kneels. Behind a slab the size of a table, half hidden by shadow, a rusted plate of iron is set into the base of the wall. The keyhole is full of dust. He blows it clear, and fits the brass key, and turns it. The lock gives with a groan like a throat clearing.

The door opens inward on dark.

He goes through it sideways, wriggling, with the lantern held out ahead of him. Beyond lies a narrow passage cut in the live rock, cold and dry, sloping upward. He climbs it for what seems like an hour. His breath smokes in the lamplight. At the top is a second door, wooden this time, rotten with age, and when he leans his weight on it, it falls outward with a crash that seems to him loud enough to wake the mountain.

He stands in the open air.

Stars. A wind from the north, with teeth in it. The black wall of the Sect rising behind him, the great curve of the Inner Court's roofs, the faint gold flicker of the fortieth landing's lantern far above. And before him, running down the slope in the starlight like a gray ribbon, the northern road.

Fourteenth night of the tenth month, he thinks. And I am a disciple of the Azure Cloud Sect, absent without leave.

The Law has a word for it. He doesn't say it aloud.

* * *

He walks until dawn, and does not stop, and does not look back. His breath is a white cloud in front of him. His boots, which he has oiled twice, are stiff with frost. The road is empty, and the emptiness is a kind of company, so that by the second hour he is walking in rhythm with his own heartbeat and listening to the silence as one listens to music.

The road runs north along the shoulder of the mountain, cut into the slope in long switchbacks, paved here and there with old flagstones and elsewhere with frozen mud. It is the road the Sect's carters use to take grain to the border villages, and the track is rutted deep. In the first hour he passes a wayside shrine with a bowl of frozen rice at its feet. In the second, a toll-house with its shutters barred and a dog barking inside. He slips by it on the verge, keeping to the shadow of the pines. In the third hour the sky begins to lighten in the east, a thin cold lemon streak behind the ridge, and the stars go out one by one.

He eats a strip of dried persimmon, standing, and puts a Warm-heart pill under his tongue.

It tastes of cinnamon and iron. The heat goes down his throat and spreads through his chest like a lit coal. He closes his eyes, and feels it creep along his channels, loosening the stiffness in his knees, the ache behind his breastbone. It is not Qi. It is a plain medicine. But it is the difference between a man who can walk and a man who can't.

Eleven left, he thinks. One a day. Eleven days of road.

Cold, says Pebble sleepily, from inside his collar. Not as cold. Thank you.

"Thank Bai."

Bai is rude. A pause. Bai is good rude.

He nearly laughs. It surprises him. He has not laughed since the Tan courtyard.

By midday he is in open country. The mountain has fallen away behind, and the land opens out into a broad shallow valley of gray fields and bare orchards, with a river curling through the middle of it like a dropped thread. A few hamlets sit along the water, smoke rising from their roofs. He avoids them. He cuts across the fields, over frozen furrows, toward a village he can see by its smoke.

* * *

He buys bread in the village at noon, and learns he was not the first to ask the way.

It is a hamlet of a dozen houses on the river, with a well and a bare tree and a woman selling flat loaves from a basket by the road. He comes up the lane with the hood of his cloak drawn low, and a copper in his fist. She weighs him with one look. She is old and square and brown, with a scarf bound over her gray hair and a face that has watched a great many travelers go by.

"Two," she says, and holds out the loaves.

"One is enough."

"You are thin. Take two." She wraps them in a cloth. "You are from the mountain."

He says nothing.

"I can tell by the walk. You people stamp." She takes his copper and bites it. "There was another from the mountain yesterday. On a gray horse. In silver and black, like a funeral." She tucks the coin in her apron. "He asked after a boy in a gray cloak, with a small animal. I said I had seen no one."

His throat tightens.

"Why?"

"Because he did not buy bread." She shrugs. "A man who does not buy bread is a man I do not help. It is a rule." Her eyes are shrewd. "You have a long way to go."

"North."

"The Gray Peak road forks at the dead oak. Take the left. The right goes to the toll, and the toll is watched." She hands him the cloth. "Eat as you walk. And do not stop at the inn at the river bend. It has a new landlord."

He bows to her, deeply. She waves a hand, as though at a fly.

He eats half a loaf as he walks, and is surprised to find he is weeping a little, for no good reason, from the plain warmth of the bread.

* * *

The riders come at the ninth hour, in the afternoon, in file along the road.

He hears them before he sees them: hooves on frozen mud, the creak of leather, a low voice calling a halt. He is crossing a stubble field a quarter mile from the road, and there is no cover. A bare field, a gray sky, and a long straight track with six riders on it.

Six gray horses. Six hooded riders in silver and black.

He drops flat in a furrow and draws the cloak over him. It is a gray cloak against gray earth, but a man lying in a field is a man lying in a field. They need only turn their heads.

The Door, he thinks.

He has practiced it for months in the dark of his cell, but never in daylight, never with a hunter in sight. He closes his eyes. He draws his breath out until it is a single thread. Ring by ring he sinks the Qi down from his channels into the six-sided base, until the river is a pool and the pool is a seed. His heart slows. Four a minute. Three. The cold of the earth comes up through his ribs and he lets it, and the world dwindles to a small dark point and goes quiet.

```
DORMANCY (Door in Winter, stage 1).
Qi signature: 3%. Heartbeat: 4/min.
Duration limit: 2 hours.
```

The riders reach the place opposite him and stop.

He cannot see them. He cannot hear. But some small awake corner of himself, the part that does not breathe, feels the pressure of their attention like a hand held over a flame. It travels across the field. It pauses on the cloak. It moves on.

It comes back.

It waits, a long time.

Then, from a great distance, a voice says: Nothing. And another: Move on. And the hooves recede.

He does not move for an hour more. When he rises, at last, at the end of two hours, he cannot feel his hands, and the sky has gone dark, and a thin rain of ice is falling. The cost lands on him all at once: numbness to the elbow, blurred sight, a roaring in his ears. He stumbles to a hedge, and finds a hollow under it, and sleeps there with his back against a stone and the cloak around him.

Three hours of numbness, he thinks, as he drops. And they were so close.

* * *

When he wakes, the light is low and red, and he knows that he is being followed.

He does not see anyone. He doesn't hear anyone either. But he has spent two years learning to feel the shape of a place, and the hollow under the hedge has changed. The wind has shifted. There is a silence in the hedge that was not there before, like the silence in a room when someone has stopped talking.

Pebble is rigid against his throat.

Wrong, it whispers. Seam. Wrong. Moving.

"Where?"

Behind. Many steps. Slow. A shiver passes through the little body. Cold smell. Like Mu.

His blood chills. He keeps his eyes closed. He breathes slowly, evenly, as Kuang has taught him, as the Door in Winter has taught him, and lets his Qi sense reach outward ring by ring through the dusk. At first there is nothing. The hedge. The frozen furrows. A crow, asleep in a bare apple tree.

Then, forty paces back along the road he walked, a point of cold.

It is faint and slow and perfectly steady. It is the temperature of a body that has been dead for some time and has decided not to notice. It moves along the verge at the pace of a walking man, and every few paces it stops, as though to listen.

Blood Shadow, he thinks. Rill-grade, from the feel. Foundation Early at most.

Pool-grade was Mu. Rill is the rank below. Not a Founder-level threat. A hunter, a tracker, a thing sent to follow and report and, if the opportunity offers, to kill. He has the Seam Needle, which Pebble can aim, and the Seal, which is weak. He has a staff, a knife, and forty-five CE of Interface reserve that he can spend in a pinch. He does not have a Veil. He does not have the Spring Vein, which sleeps.

And I am a long day's walk from the Sect, with no leave, in the dusk.

Think, he tells himself. Do not run. A running man is a seen man.

He opens his eyes. In the red light, the hedge looks like a long black wound. He rolls to his knees. And with the slow care of someone breaking a nest of wasps, he slides the cloak off his shoulders, leaves it lying in the hollow in the shape of a sleeping man, and slips away along the hedge in the opposite direction.

* * *

The Blood Shadow finds the cloak first.

He watches it from sixty paces, from the cover of a half-frozen drainage ditch with a layer of snow-crust over its lip. The creature comes out of the dusk on the verge, a tall thin shape in a gray hood, and stops at the edge of the hollow. Its head turns. It doesn't move for a long time.

Then it bends and lifts the cloak with two fingers, and shakes it, and drops it again.

It is a man, or was one. The face under the hood is the color of tallow, drawn tight over the bone, with eyes like two drops of black ink. A faint bloom of something dark clings to its hands, the dried mark of a blood-thread, flaking in the cold. Its robe is torn. It carries no sword. It walks as though its feet are a long way from its head.

It knows, Jian thinks. It knew from the first step. This is theater.

The Blood Shadow turns its head and looks directly at the ditch.

"Gate Bearer," it says.

The voice is soft, rasping, almost conversational. It does not rise. It carries across the sixty paces as easily as a whisper in a bedroom.

"You are a long way from your mountain."

Jian doesn't answer. He lies in the ditch with the staff under him and his hand on the knife.

"I have no wish to harm you." The creature spreads its long hands, palms up. "I am an errand-runner. A messenger. I carry an invitation from a house that would like very much to speak with you. It has watched you for a long time. It is concerned for your safety."

The Registry, he thinks.

"The house says: You have walked out of the Sect without leave. You have a letter. You are going to a place you ought not to go. The house says: Come home." The black eyes glitter. "It is a very kind house. It will forgive a great deal."

"Tell the house," says Jian, rising slowly from the ditch with the staff in his hands, "that I am grateful. And that I have a prior engagement."

The creature smiles. It is the thinnest of smiles, with too many teeth.

"I thought you might say that."

It moves.

* * *

It is fast. Not so fast as Shen Yuhang, but faster than anything that moves like that has a right to be.

The long hand flicks out, and a thread of black light uncoils from its fingertips like a lash. Jian throws himself sideways. The lash cracks across the frozen ground where he was standing and leaves a trench in the earth a hand deep. He rolls. He's on his feet with the staff up. The second lash takes the staff out of his hands and leaves it spinning end over end in the dusk.

Seam, thinks Jian. Pebble.

The pangolin is already moving. It clambers up his arm, onto his shoulder, snout pointed at the Blood Shadow's chest, and he feels the seam-sense open like a window in the back of his skull: the creature's body laid out in lines of weakness, the black thread cords knotted at the sternum, the cold seam at the base of the throat where the collar of the hood meets the skin. A hairline. A place where the body was stitched together after a death, and never quite closed.

The Seam Needle is a thin silver thread of Qi, no thicker than a hair. He's practiced it on straw dummies and sandstone and, once, a Blood Shadow's pelvis. He forms it in his right hand, a bright cold line in the dusk, and throws.

It goes true.

It strikes the creature at the base of the throat, in the seam, and passes through like light through a window. For a moment nothing happens. The Blood Shadow stands with its mouth slightly open, its black eyes wide, and a look of puzzled surprise crosses its face. Then it makes a small dry sound, like a twig breaking, and its legs fold.

It drops to its knees in the frost. Its head falls forward. The black thread on its hands flickers once, twice, and goes out.

Jian stands over it, gasping, with the staff gone and his heart going like a drum.

Dead, he thinks. It was so easy.

He bends over the body, and the sight of it steadies him. The face is young, under the tallow. Nineteen, perhaps. Twenty. A boy who was taken, and stitched, and sent. There is a wooden tag on a cord around the thin neck, and he lifts it with two fingers. A number, burned into the grain: 41. Nothing else. No name. He thinks of Mu, whose blade now hangs in a Garden forge, and of the Wellmaster, and of a line in a black book, and the anger that rises in him is slow and cold and has nowhere to go.

Whoever you were, he thinks, I am sorry.

He lets the tag fall.

And that's when he feels the second cold.

* * *

It comes from behind him, from the road.

He turns, and there are three more.

They stand in a line along the verge, in the last red light: tall, thin, hooded, silent. Their hands hang loose. Their faces are shadowed. Each carries, wound around one wrist, a loose coil of black thread that moves a little in the wind. He didn't feel them. He should have. He thinks, with a sick lurch: The first one was not a messenger. It was bait. It was meant to be killed. Its job was to make me sure.

Registry, he thinks. They knew I'd check for more. They sent four. They wanted me to feel safe after one.

"Thank you for the show," says the middle shadow, in the same soft voice. "We needed to see how you fight."

He backs up a step. The frozen ground crunches. Behind him, the ditch; beyond it, the open fields and the first stars. He has the knife. He has Pebble. He has a Seam Needle that costs five CE a throw, and forty left.

Eight throws, he thinks. If I'm lucky, if each one hits the throat. If they don't dodge.

The shadows begin to walk.

They don't hurry. They fan out across the road, one to the left, one to the right, one down the center, a slow, patient, killing pace. The threads uncoil from their wrists and trail on the ground behind them, rippling, like the tails of eels.

He throws the second needle. It strikes the left-hand shadow in the chest and goes in, but the creature doesn't fall. It staggers. Its mouth opens, and a thin black fluid runs from the corner. It keeps coming.

The third needle misses, because the shadow ducks, and costs him eight points all the same.

The fourth hits the center one's shoulder and sticks.

CE: 23, the panel says in the corner of his eye, in small calm letters, and he understands that he has been counting wrongly. The needle costs more at range. It costs more when he is afraid. His reserve is falling twice as fast as he thought.

And there are three of them, still walking.

* * *

He does what he has promised himself he will never do.

He turns, and runs.

Not away from them. Along the edge of the ditch, toward the hedge, toward the one thing that might give him a living thing to draw from. He crashes through the frozen branches of the hedge with the shadows behind him. The thorns tear his sleeves and his face. He's through. He falls to his knees in a field of stubble, in the blue dusk, and slaps his left hand flat on the frozen earth.

Spring Vein.

It's dead. It's been dead for three weeks. The dormancy is as plain as the cold in the ground: no root, no moss, no seed. Nothing here is alive enough to answer. But the shadows are forty paces off, closing, and the only thing in the field with life in it is the man on his knees.

He knows what that means. The Interface told him on the first day, in plain flat letters. Source destroyed. The Vein takes what is near. It takes without asking.

One draw, he thinks. Just one. Enough to make a wall. Enough to survive.

He pushes.

For a moment, nothing. Then the Spring Vein wakes like a snake in a bag.

It's not green. It's black. A line of black fire runs up his arm from the wrist to the elbow, a sheet of cold that is somehow also a scald, and the whole of the world goes white and silent. He feels it reaching. Not outward, into the soil. Inward. Into the marrow of his own arm. Into the bone.

Source: operator (self). Consumed.

He screams. He hears it from a long way off. The air above the field ripples, and a wave of gray force rolls out from his palm across the stubble, and the three shadows stagger as if struck by a wall. The nearest goes to its knees. The second throws up its arms. The third is thrown back ten paces and lies still.

But the force is cold, and it goes on pouring out, and he can't stop it.

Stop, he thinks. Stop. Stop.

He can't stop. The Vein is a mouth, and it's drinking the arm, the shoulder, the heart. He sees his own hand, gray as old bone, the veins standing out in black threads. He feels the cold climbing his throat.

The panel flares in the corner of his sight, red and quick.

```
WARNING: SPRING VEIN — SELF-DRAW.
Dormant (below freezing): draw is unsafe.
Source: operator. Marrow loss: 7%. Vital: 61%.
RECOMMEND: STOP.
EMERGENCY: sever link? (CE 20)
```

Yes, he thinks. Yes. Yes.

The link snaps. It is like a hand letting go of a rope. The black fire gutters out, and the force dies, and he falls forward on his face in the stubble with the taste of copper in his mouth.

Somewhere far off, the shadows are getting up.

He tries to rise. His left arm won't move. His legs won't answer. The world has gone very narrow and very dim, and the stars wheel overhead in the cold, and he thinks, with perfect calm: So this is how it ends.

Wake, says Pebble's small voice in his ear. Wake. Wake. Please.

He can't. He tries. He lies in the frozen furrow with his cheek against the earth, and the footsteps come closer, slow and unhurried, and he sees a pair of gray boots stop at the edge of his vision.

And a second pair. Heavier. Wearing hobnails.

A woman's voice, rough as gravel, says: "Back."

The boots with the thread-wrapped wrists don't move.

"I said back," says the voice. There is a sound like a very large hammer being lifted from an anvil. "Or I put you under the hill, and the hill has been waiting twenty years."

Nothing happens for a long moment.

Then the gray boots withdraw. One step, then another. The cold in the field eases by a degree. A pair of rough hands takes him under the arms, and lifts him, and drags him backward across the stubble toward a dark shape in the hillside that is not a hill.

A lantern comes alight. The light is a smoky yellow, and it falls on a face above him: broad, scarred, weathered the color of old leather, with gray hair cropped close and a pair of small steady eyes the same dark brown as Zhao Heng's.

"Steady, boy," says the woman. "You are in the Gray Peak mine. I am Zhao Bei. And you have just spent a good deal of your life."

Pebble's small voice is the last thing he hears: thin, terrified, and very close.

Not die, it says. Not die. Not die. I will not let.

Then he is in the dark, and the dark is warm, and there is a smell of coal smoke and wet stone, and somewhere very far away, a pick is ringing on rock.

The dark closes over him like water.
